{{short description|Hypothesis}}
{{other uses|Safety in Numbers (disambiguation)}}
[[File:Critical Mass, San Francisco, April 29, 2005.jpg|thumb|upright=1.35|[[Critical Mass (cycling)|Critical Mass]], San Francisco, April 29, 2005 and [[Muni Metro]] tram on [[J Church]] line]]

'''Safety in numbers''' is the hypothesis that, by being part of a large physical group or mass, an individual is less likely to be the victim of a mishap, [[accident]], attack, or other bad event. Some related theories also argue (and can show statistically){{Citation needed|date=June 2022}} that mass behaviour (by becoming more predictable and "known" to other people) can reduce accident risks, such as in traffic safety – in this case, the safety effect creates an actual reduction of danger, rather than just a redistribution over a larger group.

==In biology==
{{further|Selfish herd theory|Antipredator adaptation}}

The mathematical [[biologist]] [[W.D. Hamilton]] proposed his [[selfish herd theory]] in 1971 to explain why animals seek central positions in a group. Each individual can reduce its own domain of danger by situating itself with neighbours all around, so it moves towards the centre of the group.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Hamilton | first1=W. | title=Geometry for the selfish herd | journal=Journal of Theoretical Biology | volume=31 | issue=2 | pages=295–311 | date=1971 | pmid=5104951 | doi=10.1016/0022-5193(71)90189-5| bibcode=1971JThBi..31..295H }}</ref> The effect was tested in [[brown fur seal]] [[predator|predation]] by [[great white shark]]s. Using decoy seals, the distance between decoys was varied to produce different domains of danger. As predicted, the seals with a greater domain of danger had an increased risk of shark attack.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1098/rsbl.2009.0628|pmid=19793737|pmc=2817263|title=Sharks shape the geometry of a selfish seal herd: experimental evidence from seal decoys|journal=Biology Letters|volume=6|issue=1|pages=48–50|year=2010|last1=De Vos|first1=Alta|last2=O'Riain|first2=M. Justin}}</ref>  [[Antipredator adaptation]]s include behaviour such as the [[Flocking (behavior)|flocking]] of birds, herding of sheep<ref>{{cite journal |last1=King |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Wilson |first2=Alan M. |last3=Wilshin |first3=Simon D. |last4=Lowe |first4=John |last5=Haddadi |first5=Hamed |last6=Hailes |first6=Stephen |last7=Morton |first7=A. Jennifer |author7-link=Jenny Morton |year=2012 |volume=22 |issue=14 |title=Selfish-herd behaviour of sheep under threat |journal=Current Biology |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2012.05.008 |pmid=22835787 |pages=R561–R562|s2cid=208514093 |url=https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1366736/1/1366736.pdf |doi-access=free |bibcode=2012CBio...22.R561K }}</ref> and [[Shoaling and schooling|schooling]] of fish.<ref name=j12>{{cite journal |last=Orpwood |first=James E. |author2=Magurran, Anne E. |author3=Armstrong, John D. |author4=Griffiths, Siân W. |title=Minnows and the selfish herd: effects of predation risk on shoaling behaviour are dependent on habitat complexity |journal=Animal Behaviour |year=2008 |volume=76 |issue=1 |pages=143–152 |doi=10.1016/j.anbehav.2008.01.016|s2cid=53177480 }}</ref> Similarly, Adelie penguins wait to jump into the water until a large enough group has assembled, reducing each individual's risk of seal predation.<ref name=j13>{{cite book |last=Alcock |first=John |title=Animal Behavior: An Evolutionary Approach |year=2001 |publisher=Sinauer Associates |location=Sunderland, MA }}</ref> This behavior is also seen in [[Mast (botany)|masting]] and [[predator satiation]] where the predators are overwhelmed with an abundance of prey during a period of time resulting in more of the prey surviving.

==In road traffic safety==
[[File:Fietsdemonstratie in Amsterdam tegen de autoterreur, ongeveer 15.000 deelnemer, Bestanddeelnr 932-1612.jpg|thumb|[[Amsterdam]], 1982]]
In 1949 [[Reuben Smeed|R. J. Smeed]] reported that per capita road fatality rates tended to be lower in countries with higher rates of motor vehicle ownership.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Smeed|first=R. J.|date=1949-01-01|title=Some Statistical Aspects of Road Safety Research|jstor=2984177|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A (General)|volume=112|issue=1|pages=1–34|doi=10.2307/2984177}}</ref> This observation led to [[Smeed's law|Smeed's Law]]. Smeed's law proposes that increasing traffic volume leads to a decrease in fatalities per vehicle.

In 2003 Peter L. Jacobsen<ref name=":0" /> compared rates of walking and cycling, in a range of countries, with rates of collisions between motorists and cyclists or walkers. He found an inverse relationship. [[Correlation does not imply causation]]. If greater safety results in more walking and cycling, then improved safety would precede rates of walking or cycling. Jacobsen hypothesised that the correlation could be explained by 'behavioural adaptation', whereby drivers who are exposed to greater numbers of cyclists on the road begin to drive more safely around them. He concluded that "A motorist is less likely to collide with a person walking and bicycling if more people walk or bicycle." He described this theory as "safety in numbers."<ref name=":0" /> This concept has not been empirically validated. It is superficially for cycling advocates. But "Safety in numbers" ([[Smeed's law|Smeed's Law]]) can also be used to argue for increased rates of car travel. Other combined modelling<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Thompson|first1=Jason|last2=Savino|first2=Giovanni|last3=Stevenson|first3=Mark|date=2015-02-17|title=Reconsidering the Safety in Numbers Effect for Vulnerable Road Users: An Application of Agent-Based Modeling|journal=Traffic Injury Prevention|volume=16|issue=2|pages=147–153|doi=10.1080/15389588.2014.914626|issn=1538-9588|pmid=24761795|s2cid=25074848|url=https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/1007605 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Thompson|first1=Jason|last2=Wijnands|first2=Jasper S.|last3=Savino|first3=Giovanni|last4=Lawrence|first4=Brendan|last5=Stevenson|first5=Mark|date=2017-08-01|title=Estimating the safety benefit of separated cycling infrastructure adjusted for behavioral adaptation among drivers; an application of agent-based modelling|journal=Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour|volume=49|pages=18–28|doi=10.1016/j.trf.2017.05.006|bibcode=2017TRPF...49...18T |issn=1369-8478}}</ref> and empirical evidence suggests that while changes in driver behaviour might still be one way that collision risk per cyclist declines with greater numbers,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Thompson|first1=Jason|last2=Savino|first2=Giovanni|last3=Stevenson|first3=Mark|date=2016-03-01|title=A model of behavioural adaptation as a contributor to the safety-in-numbers effect for cyclists|journal=Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice|volume=85|pages=65–75|doi=10.1016/j.tra.2015.12.004|bibcode=2016TRPA...85...65T |issn=0965-8564}}</ref> the effect can be easily produced through simple spatial processes (traffic design) akin to the biological herding processes described above.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Thompson|first1=Jason Hugh|last2=Wijnands|first2=Jasper S.|last3=Mavoa|first3=Suzanne|last4=Scully|first4=Katherine|last5=Stevenson|first5=Mark R.|date=2019-10-01|title=Evidence for the 'safety in density' effect for cyclists: validation of agent-based modelling results|url=https://injuryprevention.bmj.com/content/25/5/379|journal=Injury Prevention|language=en|volume=25|issue=5|pages=379–385|doi=10.1136/injuryprev-2018-042763|issn=1353-8047|pmid=30315090|hdl=11343/224043|s2cid=52977216|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Safety in numbers is also used to describe the evidence that the number of pedestrians or cyclists correlates inversely with the risk of a motorist colliding with a [[pedestrian]] or [[cyclist]]. This non-linear relationship was first shown at intersections.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Brüde, U., Larsson, J. | year =1993 | title=Models for predicting accidents at junctions where pedestrians and cyclists are involved. How well do they fit? | journal=Accident Analysis and Prevention | pmid=8397652 | volume =25 | issue=5 | pages =499–509 | doi=10.1016/0001-4575(93)90001-D | quote=According to results obtained, the risk - the number of accidents involving unprotected road users per unprotected road user - increases with increasing numbers of motor vehicles but decreases with increasing numbers of pedestrians and cyclists.| url =https://vti.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:672186/FULLTEXT01 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=Leden, L., Gårder, P., Pulkkinen, U. | year =2000 | title=An expert judgment model applied to estimating the safety effect of a bicycle facility | journal=Accident Analysis and Prevention | volume =32 | issue=4 | pages=589–599 | doi=10.1016/S0001-4575(99)00090-1 | quote=An analysis of the relationship between bicycle flow and the number of reported accidents in the experimental area shows that the relative risk — when risk is defined as the number of expected (reportable) accidents per passing bicyclist — decreases with increasing bicycle flow | pmid=10868762 }}</ref> It has been confirmed by ecologic data from cities in California and Denmark, and European countries, and time-series data for the United Kingdom and the Netherlands.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | author =Jacobsen, P. L. | year =2003 | title=Safety in numbers: more walkers and bicyclists, safer walking and bicycling | journal =Injury Prevention | volume =9 | issue =3 | pages =205–209 |doi=10.1136/ip.9.3.205 | pmid=12966006 | pmc =1731007 | quote=A motorist is less likely to collide with a person walking and bicycling if more people walk or bicycle.}}</ref> The number of pedestrians or bicyclists injured increases at a slower rate than would be expected based on their numbers. That is, more people walk or cycle where the risk to the individual pedestrian or bicyclist is lower.<ref>{{cite journal | author =Elvik, R. | year =2009 | title=The non-linearity of risk and the promotion of environmentally sustainable transport | journal =Accident Analysis and Prevention | volume=41 | issue=4 | pages =849–855 |doi=10.1016/j.aap.2009.04.009 | pmid =19540975 | quote=Several studies show that the risks of injury to pedestrians and cyclists are highly non-linear. This means that the more pedestrians or cyclists there are, the lower is the risk faced by each pedestrian or cyclist.}}</ref><ref name="OverkillPlzFixme" /> A 2002 study into whether pedestrian risk decreased with pedestrian flow, using 1983-86 data from signalized intersections in a town in Canada, found that in some circumstances pedestrian flow increased where the risk per pedestrian decreased.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Leden, L. | year =2002 | title=Pedestrian risk decrease with pedestrian flow. A case study based on data from signalized intersections in Hamilton, Ontario | journal=Accident Analysis and Prevention | pmid=12067108 | volume=34 | issue=4 | pages =457–464 | doi=10.1016/S0001-4575(01)00043-4 | quote=When risks for pedestrians were calculated as the expected number of reported pedestrian accidents per pedestrian, risk decreased with increasing pedestrian flows and increased with increasing vehicle flow.
}}</ref>

The number of people cycling along Canberra's [[Northbourne Avenue]] between 7.30am and 9am trebled to 121 in 2005, from 40 in 2004<ref>{{Cite book |title=Cycling Cordon Count Civic and Acton 2004 to 2008 |publisher=Pedal Power ACT |year=2008 |location=Canberra}}</ref>, following completion of an on-road cycle lane. This supports the hypothesis that improved cycling safety causes the rate of cycling to increase.

After cycling was promoted in Finland, there was a 75% drop in cyclists deaths and the number of trips increased by 72%.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:norden:org:diva-1870|title=CBA of Cycling|date=2005|publisher=Nordic Council of Ministers}}</ref>

In England, between 2000 and 2008, serious bicycle injuries declined by 12%. Over the same period, the number of bicycle trips made in London doubled.<ref>{{cite journal | year=2004 | title=The London Cycling Action Plan. Transport for London, London, UK | journal=Transport for London |url=http://www.tfl.gov.uk/assets/downloads/businessandpartners/cycling-action-plan.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | year=2008 | title=Cycling in London: Final report. Transport for London, London | journal=Transport for London | url=http://www.tfl.gov.uk/assets/downloads/businessandpartners/cycling-in-london-final-october-2008.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | year=2008 | title=Central London congestion charging: Impacts monitoring, Sixth Annual Report. Transport for London, London | journal=Transport for London | url=http://www.tfl | access-date=2020-03-29 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130711142429/http://tfl/ | archive-date=2013-07-11 | url-status=dead }}</ref> Motor vehicle traffic decreased by 16%, bicycle use increased by 28% and cyclist injuries had decreased by 20% in the first year of operation of the [[London congestion charge]].<ref>{{cite web | url =http://www.tfl.gov.uk/assets/downloads/corporate/ThirdAnnualReportFinal.pdf | author=Transport for London | title =Congestion Charging: Third Annual Monitoring Report |date=April 2005}}</ref>
In January 2008, the number of cyclists in London being treated in hospitals for serious injuries had increased by 100% in six years.  Over the same time, they report, the number of cyclists had increased by 84%.<ref>{{cite news |title=Number of cyclists treated for serious injuries doubles |author=Nicholas Cecil |date=2008-01-28 |newspaper=Evening Standard |url=https://www.standard.co.uk/hp/front/number-of-cyclists-treated-for-serious-injuries-doubles-6677471.html |access-date=2008-01-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080129040843/http://www.thisislondon.co.uk/standard/article-23434443-details/Number+of+cyclists+treated+for+serious+injuries+doubles/article.do |archive-date=2008-01-29 |url-status=live }}</ref> In York, comparing the periods 1991-93 and 1996–98, the number of bicyclists killed and seriously injured fell by 59%. The share of trips made by bicycle rose from 15% to 18%.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Harrison, J. | year=2001 | title=Planning for more cycling: The York experience bucks the trend | journal=[[World Transport Policy and Practice]] | volume=7 | issue=4}}</ref>

In Germany, between 1975 and 2001, the total number of bicycle trips made in Berlin almost quadrupled. Between 1990 and 2007, the share of trips made by bicycle increased from 5% to 10%. Between 1992 and 2006, the number of serious bicycle injuries declined by 38%.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Senatsverwaltung fuer Stadtentwicklung. Office of Urban Development, Berlin, Germany | year=2003 | title=Focus on bicycling}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Pucher, J. |author2=Buehler, R. |name-list-style=amp | year=2007 | title=At the frontiers of cycling: Policy innovations in the Netherlands, Denmark, and Germany | journal=[[World Transport Policy and Practice]] | volume=13 | issue=3 | pages=8–57}}</ref> In Germany as a whole, between 1975 and 1998, cyclist fatalities fell by 66% and the percent of trips made by bicycle rose from 8% to 12%.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Pucher, J.|author2=Dijkstra, L.|name-list-style=amp|year=2000|title=Making walking and cycling safer: lessons from Europe|journal=Transportation Quarterly|volume=54|issue=3|pages=25–50|hdl=2027/mdp.39015047810828?urlappend=%3Bseq=439}}</ref>

In America, during the period 1999-2007, the absolute number of cyclists [[killed or seriously injured]] decreased by 29% and the amount of [[Cycling in New York City|cycling in New York city]] increased by 98%.<ref>{{cite journal | author=NYC DOT | year=2008 | title=Safe Streets NYC: Traffic Safety Improvements in New York City}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=A Joint Report from the New York City Departments of Health and Mental Hygiene, Parks and Recreation, Transportation, and the New York City Police Department | year=2005 | title=Bicyclist Fatalities and Serious Injuries in New York City 1996-2005}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | title=New York City Commuter cyclist indicator | url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/downloads/pdf/commuter_cycling_indicator_and_data_2009.pdf}}</ref>
In Portland, Oregon, between 1990 and 2000, the percentage of workers who commuted to work by bicycle rose from 1.1% to 1.8%. By 2008, the proportion has risen to 6.0%; while the number of workers increased by only 36% between 1990 and 2008, the number of workers commuting by bicycle increased 608%. Between 1992 and 2008, the number of bicyclists crossing four bridges into downtown was measured to have increased 369% between 1992 and 2008. During that same period, the number of reported crashes increased by only 14%.<ref>{{cite journal | author=US Census Bureau | year=2009 | title=U.S. Census website | url=https://www.census.gov | access-date=2020-03-29 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=City of Portland, Portland Bureau of Transportation | year=2008 | title= Portland bicycle counts 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=City of Portland | year=2008 | title=Portland's 2008 bicycle friendly community application, Portland, OR}}</ref>

In Copenhagen, Denmark, between 1995 and 2006, the number of cyclists killed or seriously injured fell by 60%. During the same period, cycling increased by 44% and the percent of people cycling to work increased from 31% to 36%.<ref>{{cite journal | author=City of Copenhagen Traffic Department | year=2007 | title=Copenhagen, city of cyclists: bicycle account 2006 | url=http://www.vejpark2.kk.dk/publikationer/pdf/464_Cykelregnskab_UK.%202006.pdf | access-date=2010-10-14 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719125945/http://www.vejpark2.kk.dk/publikationer/pdf/464_Cykelregnskab_UK.%202006.pdf | archive-date=2011-07-19 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

In the Netherlands, between 1980 and 2005, and cyclist fatalities decreased by 58% and cycling increased by 45%.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Ministerie van Verkeer en Waterstaat | year=2007 | title=Cycling in the Netherlands}}</ref>

During 7 years of the 1980s, admissions to hospital of cyclists declined by 5% and cycling in Western Australia increased by 82%.
<ref>{{cite journal | author=Robinson, D. | year=2005 | title=Safety in numbers in Australia: more walkers and bicyclists, safer walking and bicycling | journal=Health Promotion Journal of Australia | volume=16 | issue=1 | pages=47–51 | url=https://www.cycle-helmets.com/hpja_2005_1_robinson.pdf | pmid=16389930 | doi=10.1071/he05047}}</ref>
